newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem tries to hurry Argentine labor reforms.
newsitem.headline: Menem tries to hurry Argentine labor reforms.

text.p: President Carlos Menem urged Congress Monday to rush through a package of labor law reforms which he insists are the key to securing new loans for Argentina from international credit organizations.

The Peronist president, speaking on local radio, asked members of Congress to "do their best for these bills to get passed quickly", arguing that "it will give us the possibility of getting lots of credit, from among others, the World Bank."

Menem's labor reforms, which he insists are the best way to combat unemployment and which the World Bank has offered to facilitate with financial aid, are bogged down in Congress and he is threatening to pass them by decree.
The parliamentary term has already ended and there are only four extraordinary sessions left until the end of the year, two of which fall on Christmas and New Year holidays.
Peronist whip Jorge Matzkin warns of little time and less consensus. He spoke last week of "hardly one point of agreement" among the government, unions and business.
The Radical Party's Shadow Labor Minister Alfredo Allende told Reuters it was increasingly likely Menem would give up on Congress and push through the reforms using special powers.
"He'll probably use his power of decree," said Allende.

It was unclear whether Matzkin would try to get deputies to debate the labor bills in Wednesday's session, especially since the Radicals protest that a draft bill issued by the lower house's Labor Committee late last month is not legitimate because it was not voted on by the full committee.

That draft attempts to bundle together various government proposals into an "employment emergency" law, giving employers two years' grace to hire new workers with six-month contracts, renewable for two years, on reduced social benefits.

It would also replace redundancy payouts with unemployment insurance to be financed by companies. Separate bills aim to scrap union-controlled collective wage deals and loosen up regulations on working hours and conditions.

The imminent release of fresh jobs data expected to show no improvement in the 17.1 percent jobless rate gives new impetus to the labor debate. Another reason for the rush is mid-term elections next year, leaving little space for unpopular reforms ahead of the presidential election in 1999.
"It will be one long election campaign from 1997 to 1999," says Argentine economist Miguel Angel Broda.

There is little doubt that high labor costs are a major concern for businesses as they try to climb out of recession. A Price Waterhouse poll shows labor legislation is their top concern, above the legal system or unemployment.

But unions and opposition insist labor "flexibilization" will not resolve unemployment or boost businesses. "This kind of law will not change the economic outlook or the labor situation," said the Radicals' Alfredo Allende.
But the government insists that economic recovery alone cannot address the employment problem.

"Employment responds much more to a reduction in labor costs than to an increase in GDP," said Carola Pessino, a labor consultant to Economy Minister Roque Fernandez at a recent employment seminar. "Growth policies are not enough."

FIEL consultancy estimates each one percent rise in gross domestic product means a 0.4 percent drop in unemployment, so even if economic growth in 1997 hits the 5.0 percent target, the impact on the jobless rate would not be dramatic.
Radical economist Ricardo Lopez Murphy says the real solution is reduced payroll taxes -- but tight fiscal goals leave little room for such a move.
